title: Harvard Law Bars International Students From Externship Clinics Under New Guidance
excerpt: August federal guidance says Curricular Practical Training can be authorised only if the training is required of every student in the programme. Harvard's externships fail that test, closing all 13 clinics to international J.D. students.
body:
• Harvard Law School will no longer authorise international J.D. students for externship clinics this academic year, after August federal guidance narrowed Curricular Practical Training.
  • The mechanism: CPT may now be authorised only if the training is required of all students in the degree programme — and Harvard externships are not, because students can meet the experiential requirement in-house.
  • All 13 externship clinics are affected; in-house clinics remain open to F-1 students, according to Harvard Law's own F-1 guidance.
  • Reader takeaway: if you are an international law student in the US, do not register for an externship until your international office confirms work authorisation in writing — and ask about in-house clinics and pre-completion OPT before you commit.

Harvard Law School has ended school authorisation for international J.D. students to take part in externship clinics this academic year, after new federal guidance narrowed when universities can approve off-campus work. The change shows how a reinterpretation of a student-visa work rule can close off placements at government agencies, companies and non-profits.

This article is based on The Harvard Crimson and Harvard Law School's published F-1 guidance — the readable sources used after the Economic Times item arrived via a Google News link.

The rule that changed

In two messages to schools in August, the Student and Exchange Visitor Program said Curricular Practical Training — CPT, a temporary work authorisation granted by schools that lets international students gain off-campus professional experience — may be authorised only if the training is required of all students in the degree programme, The Harvard Crimson reported.

https://x.com/EconomicTimes/status/2109904187719127474

Harvard Law's graduation requirements include six credits of experiential learning courses, a category that includes externship clinics. But students can also fulfil that requirement through in-house clinics and seminars. Because externships are therefore not required of every student, they no longer qualify for CPT under the new interpretation, the Crimson reported.

Which clinics are affected

The change bars international J.D. students from all 13 of the Law School's externship clinics, which pair a course component with placements at government agencies, companies and non-profit organisations. Previously, international students were barred only from some externships, such as government placements that require US citizenship, according to the Crimson.

Under previous CPT practice, students could take one semester of an externship but could not extend it, the Crimson reported.

Students in LL.M. programmes are unaffected, the Crimson reported, because they were always barred from externships: they are ineligible for CPT authorisation, which requires a full academic year of enrolment.

Harvard Law's own page for F-1 students states the position plainly: CPT authorisation is not available for externships or domestic independent clinicals, and students should not register for an externship clinic until they have conferred with the Harvard International Office contact named on that page about whether they can secure work authorisation, according to Harvard Law School.

What Harvard says, and the alternatives

Associate Dean for Academic Programs Meredith Boak said in a statement reported by the Crimson that the Law School is committed to helping students navigate the federal guidance. Boak said the school reached out to all F-1 students and was working directly with students already enrolled in externship clinics to help them understand their options, and that students unable to pursue an externship were being offered individualised advising to identify an alternative path.

Boak also pointed students to the Law School's in-house clinical programme, which the Crimson said has 25 offerings. Harvard's F-1 page confirms that all J.D. and LL.M. students in F-1 status are eligible for in-house clinics, student practice organisations, spring break pro bono projects and international independent clinical projects.

A second alternative is pre-completion Optional Practical Training — OPT, a federally granted authorisation for up to 12 months of degree-related work that students typically use after graduation. Affected J.D. students may still apply for it, the Crimson reported, and Harvard's F-1 page invites students to explore whether they could apply. The trade-off is explicit in the Crimson's reporting: using OPT for an externship would cut into the time available for work experience in the US after graduation.

What this means for Indian students

The Crimson quoted student government co-president Tenzin Yonten, a second-year international student from India who had been considering an externship, as hoping to compile information for affected students. No count of Indian students affected was given in the sources read.

For international law students elsewhere in the US, the lesson is procedural: eligibility now turns on whether your degree requires that exact training of every student. Confirm CPT eligibility before registering, keep the answer in writing, and price in the OPT trade-off. The Crimson presents Harvard's move as a response to guidance, not a school-initiated choice.
